analysis.one_liner: Taxes drug companies up to 100% of revenue from price spikes above medical inflation.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have taxed drug makers up to 100% of revenue from price increases above medical inflation, never got a hearing or vote in the Senate Finance Committee before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would put a new tax on brand-name drug companies whenever they raise a drug's price faster than the medical care inflation rate. The tax would take 50% to 100% of the extra revenue from the price increase, depending on how big the spike was, and it would also apply to companies that have pushed prices up year after year. Drug companies would have to report prices, sales, and their justification for increases to the HHS Inspector General every quarter, and the report would be made public. Companies could get out of the tax only if they showed a real reason, like higher manufacturing costs, or if the drug is a cheap generic-style product sold by many competitors. Money raised would go to the National Institutes of Health for drug research.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients, families, and employers who pay for prescription drugs, plus Medicare and Medicaid, because the tax makes big price increases immediately costly. The public record of which companies raised prices and why would also help regulators, insurers, and shoppers. Money collected would fund NIH drug research.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and everyone paying for prescriptions

how_it_helps.text: Imposes an excise tax of 50% of the extra revenue from a price spike (75% for spikes of 15% or more, 100% for spikes of 20% or more), whenever a drug's price rises faster than the medical care inflation index [S2] [S3].

Covers repeated gouging, not just single-year spikes: a cumulative tax applies when a drug's price is far above its base-year price, with rates reaching 100% for compounds like 107% over four years [S3].

Requires drug companies to report prices, sales, and justifications to the HHS Inspector General quarterly, with civil penalties of 0.5% to 1% of a drug's annual gross revenue per day of delay, and publishes the assessments (minus trade secrets) [S3].

Protects legitimate increases: companies can win an exemption for input cost increases, and revenue due solely to higher manufacturing costs is subtracted from the tax base; cheap drugs (under $10 per 30-day supply) sold by at least three competitors are exempt [S2] [S3].
Closes a known workaround by counting a drug with a trivial 'reformulation' as the same drug as the original version [S3].
Directs that revenue collected be appropriated to NIH for drug research and development [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug companies that raise prices faster than medical inflation. They would lose 50% to 100% of the revenue gained from each spike, face quarterly reporting duties with per-day penalties, and lose the pricing power that comes from opaque, unexplained increases.

drawbacks.text: The tax is on revenue, not profit, so a company with thin margins on a spiked drug could owe the government more than the increase earned; supporters of the bill would accept this as the cost of deterrence, but it is a real risk of unintended harm [S3].

The thresholds create games: a company might take one large increase and then hold prices flat, or spread increases just under the allowance, since only spikes above medical inflation trigger the tax [S3].
The bill does nothing about launch prices for new drugs, which are often the biggest cost problem; it only orders a Government Accountability Office study of how initial prices are set [S2] [S3].

For-cause exemptions are discretionary and would put the HHS Secretary in the position of judging manufacturing-cost claims, creating an administrative bottleneck and litigation risk, though the bill bars companies from using threats to curtail production as grounds for an exemption [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: it leaves ordinary price increases (those tracking medical inflation) untouched and taxes only large or repeated spikes, while carving out cheap, competitive drugs and genuine cost-driven increases. The main weaknesses are that a revenue-based tax can overtax low-margin drugs and that it sidesteps the larger problem of high launch prices for new drugs. On balance it is a reasonable design for the narrow problem it takes on, but it only addresses part of drug pricing.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Sen. Sherrod Brown introduced the bill on June 15, 2017, joined by five Senate Democrats as original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
Eight senators in total signed on as cosponsors, seven Democrats and one Independent; no Republican did [S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance on the day of introduction [S5].
That referral was the last action ever taken; no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded for the rest of the 115th Congress [S5].
Congress ended on January 3, 2019, so the bill died in committee without ever reaching the Senate floor [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug companies kept their freedom to raise prices above medical inflation without a new tax, public reporting of spike revenue, or per-day penalties for withholding data. No one else gained anything from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Sherrod Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Price Gouging Act and brought it to the Senate floor for introduction.

for.name: 8 Senate cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors, including Sens. Gillibrand, Franken, Reed, Hassan, and Udall as original cosponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day of introduction and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.role: Majority party controlling the Senate agenda
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor, which it could not reach without committee action; no Republican cosponsored it.

sides.party_line_note: All nine sponsors were Democrats or an Independent — no Republican signed on — and with no hearing or vote ever held, the record shows no Republican support at any stage.

industries.note: The bill would take 50-100% of the revenue from any price increase above the medical inflation rate, hit companies again for prices already far above their base-year levels, and require quarterly public reporting of prices and justifications with per-day fines for delays. The industry profits from increases above inflation, so its interest in this bill ran directly against patients and payers.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and health insurers
industries.note: Indirect beneficiary: slower drug price increases lower the costs insurers and employers pay, though the bill regulates manufacturers, not them. The GAO study would also examine how health plans help set initial drug prices.
